# Introduction to Deep Sleep  {.unnumbered}

The ESP32 is a powerful microcontroller, but with that power comes significant energy consumption. When running normally, the ESP32 draws around 40-70mA of current. If it's constantly awake reading sensors, a standard battery would be drained in just a few days.

To build an autonomous weather station that can run for months or years in the field, we must utilize **Deep Sleep**.

## What is Deep Sleep?

Deep sleep puts the ESP32 into a primitive state where almost everything shuts down:

*   The 2 main CPUs stop functioning, and the **ULP (Ultra Low Power) processor** takes over. This tiny processor consumes very little energy but can still perform basic actions.
*   Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios are completely disabled.
*   The Flash and the main system memory (RAM) are no longer powered. Only the special **RTC memory** remains active and usable.

In this state, the ESP32 consumes a mere **10µA to 150µA**! 

### RAM Erasure and RTC_DATA_ATTR

Because the main CPU and RAM are unpowered during deep sleep, all standard variables saved in RAM are completely erased. 

Fortunately, the RTC RAM remains powered. If we need to keep track of data across deep sleep cycles (for example, storing a boot counter to track how many times the ESP32 has woken up), we can force the ESP32 to save the variable in this special memory by adding the `RTC_DATA_ATTR` attribute to its declaration.

### The Deep Sleep Paradigm (`setup` vs `loop`)

In Phase 01, our code relied on the standard Arduino structure: we initialized our sensors in the `setup()` function once, and then continuously took measurements and called `delay()` inside the `loop()` function.

Deep sleep completely changes this paradigm. When the ESP32 wakes up from deep sleep, it resets. The `setup()` function runs from the very beginning, and once it hits the command to go back to sleep, execution stops entirely. Therefore, in a deep sleep application, the `loop()` function is **never called**.

## Wake-up Sources

After putting the ESP32 into deep sleep, there are several ways to wake it back up. We must configure a **Wake-up Source** before telling the ESP32 to go to sleep:

### 1. Internal Timer Wake-up
The ESP32 has an internal timer in its RTC subsystem. You can tell it to sleep for a specific number of microseconds, and it will automatically wake itself up when the time expires.

Here is a quick "Hello Deep Sleep" example using the internal timer:

```cpp
#include <Arduino.h>

// Conversion factor for micro seconds to seconds
#define uS_TO_S_FACTOR 1000000ULL  
#define TIME_TO_SLEEP  10          // Sleep for 10 seconds

void setup(){
  Serial.begin(115200);
  delay(1000); 
  
  Serial.println("Waking up! Reading sensors...");
  // ... (Your sensor code would go here) ...
  
  Serial.println("Going to sleep for 10 seconds.");
  Serial.flush(); 
  
  // Configure the timer wake-up
  esp_sleep_enable_timer_wakeup(TIME_TO_SLEEP * uS_TO_S_FACTOR);
  
  // Enter deep sleep
  esp_deep_sleep_start();
}

void loop(){
  // This is never reached because esp_deep_sleep_start() halts execution!
}
```

> **Ready-to-use project:** If you don't want to copy-paste, you can directly open the complete PlatformIO project from the source code here: [`04_deep_sleep_timer`](https://github.com/wg1d/personal-autonomous-weather-station/tree/main/firmware/Phase-02/04_deep_sleep_timer)

*   **Pros:** Requires no external hardware or wiring. Extremely easy to program in software as seen above.
*   **Cons:** The internal timer is notorious for drifting, especially when temperature fluctuates (which happens a lot outdoors!). Over a few weeks, your station might wake up minutes or even hours off schedule.

### 2. Capacitive Touch Pins
The ESP32 has several pins that act as capacitive touch sensors. You can configure the ESP32 to wake up simply when a user physically touches one of these pins.

### 3. RTC Pins (External Interrupt EXT0 / EXT1)
You can configure the ESP32 to wake up when an electrical signal on a specific RTC pin changes state (e.g., goes from 3.3V down to 0V). This is perfect for waking up the ESP32 instantly when a user presses a physical button, when a magnetic hall sensor detects a door opening, or when a PIR motion sensor detects movement.

*   **Pros:** Allows an external component to dictate the schedule.
*   **Cons:** Requires additional hardware (like an external RTC module or sensor) and extra wiring.

## Why We Use the DS3231 RTC Alarms

Because weather data relies heavily on accurate timestamping, and because our station will be subjected to temperature fluctuations, we will avoid the ESP32's internal timer. 

Instead, we will use the **DS3231 RTC** we installed in Phase 01. The DS3231 contains a Temperature Compensated Crystal Oscillator (TCXO), meaning it keeps perfect time regardless of the weather. 

We will program a hardware **Alarm** inside the DS3231. When the alarm triggers, the DS3231 will pull its **SQW (Square Wave)** pin LOW. By wiring this SQW pin to our ESP32 and configuring an `EXT0` external wake-up, the DS3231 will physically "tap the ESP32 on the shoulder" and wake it up exactly when a reading is required!

In the next chapter, we will modify our hardware circuit to connect this wake-up pin and implement an additional hardware trick to save even more power.
